Lesson 4 · Business route

Regression as an explicit approximation

How should a workshop forecast completion time for a new batch?

The business problem

A workshop manager must promise completion times before new batches reach the floor. Batch size is known when a job is booked, so planners can use it to forecast labor and delivery dates. The manager’s problem is operational: a late promise can disappoint a customer, while a large safety margin can waste capacity. The team needs a rule that is accurate enough to schedule work and simple enough for planners to apply.

What the data show

A straight-line fit estimates 7.23 additional minutes per unit of batch size. The operations team then checks how forecast errors change for larger batches.

The fitted straight line gives a quick estimate of how minutes rise with batch size. The team then looks at actual times and forecast misses across the observed size range. Larger batches show a different pattern and more variation, so average fit alone is a poor basis for deadline promises. Candidate rules are compared on held-back batches using the same error measure. The smallest numerical score matters only if it improves staffing or reduces costly late jobs enough to justify extra complexity.

What would you decide?

Inspect the curve and residuals, then compare candidate forecasts on held-out data. Choose the level of complexity that improves the decision, not merely the training score.

Begin with a forecast for batches similar to those already observed and add a buffer tied to the cost of lateness. Send unusually large or unfamiliar batches for manual review. During a shadow trial, planners record their usual estimate, the model estimate, the actual finish time, and any deadline miss. Management can then adopt the rule that makes better promises in routine work, with a clear trigger for human judgment.

Pause and explain

Does a high in-sample fit make the line a reliable forecast for very large batches?

Compare your reasoning

No. The generating mean bends, and prediction beyond the observed size range needs a separate argument.

Check your judgment

Reveal the case’s known answer

The case’s completion-time curve bends as batches grow, and larger batches have more variable completion times. A size-based rule needs a buffer for deadline promises.

The bigger picture

A forecast becomes valuable when it changes an operating decision. The workshop does not need the most impressive curve; it needs dependable staffing and delivery promises. That means choosing an error measure tied to the cost of a miss, testing the rule on new batches, and defining when staff should review an unusual job. The principle applies to demand, delivery, and capacity forecasts. The next lesson asks a related question: when conditions differ across assets, which prediction or comparison should guide an investment?
